facts: Antigua is said to have 365 beaches, one for every day of the year.
The country's highest point was renamed Mount Obama in 2009 and reverted to Boggy Peak in name only locally.
Nelson's Dockyard is the only continuously working Georgian-era naval dockyard in the world.
AG.about: Two very different islands make up this state, plus the uninhabited rock of Redonda. Antigua has an indented coastline of coves and natural harbours, with older volcanic hills in the south-west and low limestone country elsewhere; Barbuda, some 40 kilometres to the north, is a flat coral island fringed by reefs, and its Codrington Lagoon shelters one of the largest frigatebird colonies in the Caribbean. English settlers arrived on Antigua in 1632 and turned it into a sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans, while Barbuda was leased for generations to the Codrington family. Independence came on 1 November 1981. The climate is relatively dry, with few permanent streams, so the country relies heavily on desalinated water. Tourism dominates the economy, and the vulnerability of low islands to Atlantic hurricanes was shown in 2017, when Hurricane Irma wrecked most buildings on Barbuda and its whole population had to be evacuated.

facts: The Bahamas is an archipelago of around 700 islands and cays, about 30 of them inhabited.
Dean's Blue Hole off Long Island is one of the deepest known underwater sinkholes.
It is one of the few countries whose highest point is under 100 metres.
BS.about: Strictly speaking, the Bahamas lies in the Atlantic rather than the Caribbean Sea. Its islands sit on the Great and Little Bahama Banks, vast shallow limestone platforms whose turquoise water is cut by deep channels such as the Tongue of the Ocean off Andros, the largest island. Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas here in 1492, and within a few decades the native Lucayan people had been carried off to labour on Hispaniola and had disappeared. English settlers from Bermuda arrived in the 1640s, Nassau became a notorious pirate haven in the early 18th century, and Loyalists fleeing the American Revolution later brought plantations and enslaved workers. The country became independent on 10 July 1973. Most Bahamians live on New Providence, while the Out Islands remain thinly settled. Tourism and offshore financial services drive the economy, and powerful hurricanes, including Dorian in 2019, pose a recurring threat to the low-lying islands.

facts: Barbados is made largely of coral limestone rather than volcanic rock, unlike most of its neighbours.
It became a republic in 2021, replacing the British monarch with a president.
Rum distilling began here in the 17th century, and Mount Gay claims to be the oldest surviving brand.
BB.about: Barbados lies apart from the rest of the eastern Caribbean, about 160 kilometres east of the Windward Islands chain, directly exposed to the Atlantic trade winds. Its west coast faces calm water and sandy beaches, while the rugged east coast around Bathsheba takes the full force of the ocean swell; inland, the eroded Scotland District contrasts with gently terraced limestone uplands riddled with caves. English settlers arrived in 1627, and unusually the island never changed colonial hands. In the 1640s it pioneered large-scale sugar planting with enslaved African labour, a model later copied across the region, and its House of Assembly, dating from 1639, is one of the oldest legislatures in the Commonwealth. Barbados became independent on 30 November 1966. Today it is among the most densely populated countries in the Americas, with an economy built on tourism, international business services and a well-educated workforce, and it has a reputation for political stability.

facts: Belize is the only country in Central America where English is the official language.
The Belize Barrier Reef is the second largest reef system in the world after Australia's.
The capital moved inland to Belmopan in 1970 after a hurricane devastated Belize City.
BZ.about: Facing the Caribbean on the eastern side of the Yucatán Peninsula, Belize is a country of low swampy coast in the north and the forested Maya Mountains in the south, with hundreds of small cays strung offshore. Out on Lighthouse Reef lies the Great Blue Hole, a near-circular marine sinkhole formed when sea levels were lower. Large Maya cities such as Caracol, Lamanai and Xunantunich flourished here long before Europeans arrived. British woodcutters, the Baymen, began exploiting logwood and later mahogany in the 17th century, and the territory became the colony of British Honduras in 1862. It was renamed Belize in 1973 and gained independence on 21 September 1981, though a long-standing Guatemalan territorial claim kept British troops there for years afterwards. It has the lowest population density in Central America, and its people include Mestizo, Creole, Maya, Garifuna and Mennonite communities, with tourism and agriculture the main economic pillars.

facts: Canada has the longest coastline of any country, at over 200,000 kilometres.
It contains more lake area than the rest of the world combined.
Its border with the United States is the longest international land border anywhere.
CA.about: Much of Canada rests on the Canadian Shield, an ancient expanse of granite and gneiss scraped bare by ice-age glaciers and left dotted with countless lakes and muskeg. Around it lie the flat Prairies, the folded Rocky and Coast Mountains of the west, the St Lawrence lowlands and the frozen islands of the Arctic Archipelago. Despite this enormous territory, most Canadians live within a couple of hundred kilometres of the southern border, where the climate is mildest. Modern Canada began with Confederation on 1 July 1867, when four British colonies united; full legislative independence followed through the Statute of Westminster in 1931 and the patriation of the constitution in 1982. The country is officially bilingual, with French predominant in Quebec, and Indigenous First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples hold distinct rights, including the self-governing territory of Nunavut, created in 1999. Its economy draws heavily on energy, minerals, forestry and hydroelectric power alongside a large service sector.

facts: Costa Rica abolished its army in 1949 and has not reinstated one.
Around a quarter of its land is protected, and it holds roughly 5% of the world's biodiversity.
It has run for long stretches on almost entirely renewable electricity.
CR.about: A backbone of volcanoes and mountain ranges runs the length of Costa Rica, including active peaks such as Arenal, Poás and Irazú. Between these ranges sits the Central Valley, a temperate upland where the majority of the population lives and where coffee became the country's first great export in the 19th century. The Pacific side, with the Nicoya Peninsula, has a pronounced dry season, while the Caribbean slope is wetter and greener all year. Costa Rica gained independence from Spain in 1821 along with the rest of Central America and went its own way after the Central American federation broke apart in the late 1830s. Banana plantations and a railway to the Caribbean port of Limón brought workers from Jamaica, whose descendants give that coast a distinct Afro-Caribbean, English-speaking heritage. Today the economy rests on tourism, especially nature tourism, along with medical-device manufacturing, services and agricultural exports such as pineapples and bananas.

facts: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, bigger than all the others combined by land area.
It has one of the highest doctor-to-population ratios in the world and exports medical staff abroad.
Old Havana preserves one of the largest collections of Spanish colonial architecture in the Americas.
CU.about: Long and narrow, the main island of Cuba stretches roughly 1,200 kilometres from west to east, flanked by thousands of cays and the Isla de la Juventud. Much of the land is fertile plain, but the Sierra Maestra rises steeply in the south-east, and the limestone towers known as mogotes give the Viñales valley in the west its distinctive scenery. Spain colonised the island from 1511 and held it far longer than most of its American possessions, as sugar and tobacco plantations worked by enslaved Africans made it immensely valuable. Wars of independence from 1868 culminated in the Spanish–American War of 1898, and Cuba became a republic in 1902 under heavy United States influence, which also left the US naval base at Guantánamo Bay. The 1959 revolution brought a communist government, and a US trade embargo has shaped the economy since the early 1960s. Tourism, nickel, tobacco and remittances are now central, and hurricanes regularly strike.

facts: Dominica is known as the Nature Island for its rainforest and volcanic terrain.
Boiling Lake is the second largest hot lake in the world, kept simmering by volcanic activity.
It has the last remaining pre-Columbian Kalinago community in the eastern Caribbean.
DM.about: Not to be confused with the Dominican Republic, Dominica is a steep, young volcanic island in the Lesser Antilles, lying between the French islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique. Its mountains catch heavy rainfall from the trade winds, feeding fast rivers, waterfalls and dense forest, and Morne Trois Pitons National Park, with fumaroles and hot springs, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Rugged terrain and fierce resistance from its Indigenous inhabitants delayed European settlement, and the island was contested by France and Britain before passing finally into British hands in the late 18th century. The French influence survives in place names and in the Kwéyòl creole widely spoken alongside English. Independence came on 3 November 1978. Deep water close inshore attracts sperm whales year-round, making whale-watching a speciality. The economy relies on agriculture, ecotourism and a citizenship-by-investment programme, and recovery from Hurricane Maria, a Category 5 storm that devastated the island in 2017, has been a defining national effort.

facts: The Dominican Republic shares the island of Hispaniola with Haiti.
Pico Duarte is the highest peak in the entire Caribbean.
Santo Domingo was the first permanent European settlement in the Americas, founded in 1496.
DO.about: Occupying the eastern two-thirds of Hispaniola, the Dominican Republic contains the Caribbean's most dramatic relief. Parallel mountain ranges, led by the Cordillera Central, enclose the fertile Cibao Valley, the country's agricultural heartland, while in the south-west the salty Lake Enriquillo lies around 40 metres below sea level, the lowest point of any Caribbean island, and is home to American crocodiles and iguanas. After three centuries as a Spanish colony, the territory was ceded to France and then ruled from Haiti between 1822 and 1844; independence is dated from 27 February 1844, when Dominicans broke away from Haitian control. Spain briefly reannexed it in the 1860s, the United States occupied it from 1916 to 1924, and the Trujillo dictatorship lasted from 1930 to 1961. Today it is one of the fastest-growing economies in Latin America, driven by beach tourism at resorts such as Punta Cana, free-trade-zone manufacturing, mining and remittances, and it supplies a remarkable share of professional baseball players.

facts: El Salvador is the smallest and most densely populated country on the Central American mainland.
It is the only Central American country with no Caribbean coastline.
In 2021 it became the first country to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender.
SV.about: Facing only the Pacific, El Salvador is dominated by a chain of volcanoes running parallel to the coast, with fertile volcanic soils between them that have long supported intensive farming. Earthquakes are frequent, and Lake Ilopango near the capital fills a caldera left by a massive eruption around the 5th or 6th century AD that buried nearby Maya settlements. The Lempa River crosses the country to the sea and supplies much of its hydroelectric power. El Salvador became independent from Spain in 1821 within the Central American federation and emerged as a separate republic after the federation collapsed around 1840. Coffee dominated the economy from the late 19th century, concentrating land in few hands and fuelling tensions that erupted into a civil war from 1980 to 1992, ended by UN-brokered peace accords. A large diaspora, mostly in the United States, sends home remittances that form a major part of the economy, which adopted the US dollar in 2001.

facts: Grenada is called the Spice Isle and is a leading producer of nutmeg and mace.
Nutmeg appears on its national flag, the only flag to feature a spice.
Its capital, St. George's, is built around a submerged volcanic crater forming the harbour.
GD.about: Three inhabited islands make up Grenada: the main island, plus Carriacou and Petite Martinique in the southern Grenadines. The main island is volcanic and mountainous, with rainforest, waterfalls and Grand Etang, a lake filling an old crater, while about eight kilometres off its north coast lies Kick 'em Jenny, one of the most active submarine volcanoes in the Caribbean. France colonised Grenada in the mid-17th century, displacing the Kalinago, before ceding it to Britain in 1763; the French briefly retook it during the American Revolutionary War. Independence followed on 7 February 1974. A revolutionary government took power in 1979, and its violent collapse in 1983 prompted a United States–led intervention. Lying near the southern edge of the hurricane belt, the island was long thought relatively safe until Hurricane Ivan damaged most of its buildings in 2004. Tourism, agriculture and a large offshore medical university are now central to the economy.

facts: Volcán Tajumulco is the highest point in the whole of Central America, and one of more than thirty volcanoes running down the country's Pacific side.
Guatemala has the largest indigenous population share in Central America, with over twenty Mayan languages spoken.
Tikal, in the northern rainforest, was one of the most powerful cities of the Maya world.
GT.about: Guatemala's southern half is a rugged volcanic highland of deep valleys and crater lakes, the most famous being Lake Atitlán, which fills a vast caldera beneath three volcanic cones. To the north, the land drops into Petén, a flat limestone lowland of tropical forest that makes up roughly a third of the country, while a narrow plain runs along the Pacific and a short stretch of coast reaches the Caribbean at the Gulf of Honduras. Spanish conquest began in 1524, and the colonial capital at what is now Antigua Guatemala was abandoned after earthquakes in 1773, which is why the modern capital stands elsewhere. Independence from Spain came in 1821, followed by membership of the Central American federation. A US-backed coup in 1954 and a civil war lasting from 1960 to 1996 shaped modern politics. Coffee, sugar, bananas and cardamom, of which Guatemala is the world's leading exporter, are mainstays, and remittances are increasingly important.

facts: Haiti became the first independent nation in Latin America and the first republic founded by former slaves, in 1804.
It shares Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic and occupies the western third.
The Citadelle Laferrière, built after independence to repel a French return, is the largest fortress in the Americas.
HT.about: The name Haiti comes from a Taíno word usually translated as 'land of high mountains', and the country is indeed one of the most mountainous in the Caribbean, with ranges separated by narrow plains and valleys and offshore islands such as Gonâve and Tortuga, once a famous buccaneer base. As the French colony of Saint-Domingue, it became in the 18th century the world's leading producer of sugar and coffee, built on the labour of hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans. The uprising that began in 1791, led by figures such as Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, ended French rule, but France later demanded a heavy indemnity in exchange for recognition, a burden that weighed on the economy for generations. The United States occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. Haitian Creole and French are the official languages. Heavy deforestation has left slopes prone to erosion, and the 2010 earthquake near Port-au-Prince caused enormous loss of life.

facts: Copán holds some of the finest Maya sculpture and hieroglyphic inscriptions known.
Honduras has the second largest section of the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, off its Bay Islands.
The Mosquitia rainforest in the east is one of the largest wilderness areas in Central America.
HN.about: Honduras is one of the most mountainous countries in Central America, its interior a jumble of ranges and highland basins. It has a long Caribbean coastline in the north, with the Bay Islands of Roatán, Utila and Guanaja offshore, but only a short Pacific shore on the Gulf of Fonseca. Independence from Spain came in 1821, and Honduras became a separate state in 1838 when the Central American federation dissolved. In the early 20th century American fruit companies built vast banana plantations along the north coast, and the country inspired the term 'banana republic'. A brief war with El Salvador in 1969, sparked partly by migration disputes and remembered as the Football War, strained regional relations. Hurricane Mitch in 1998 killed thousands and destroyed much of the country's infrastructure. Garifuna communities live along the Caribbean coast, and today's economy relies on coffee, bananas, garment assembly plants and remittances from emigrants.

facts: Jamaica is the birthplace of ska, rocksteady, reggae and dancehall, an unusual concentration of globally influential music for a country of under three million people.
Blue Mountain coffee, grown at high altitude, is among the most expensive in the world.
It has produced a remarkable number of world-record sprinters for a country of under three million people.
JM.about: The third largest island of the Greater Antilles, Jamaica rises from a narrow coastal plain to a central limestone plateau and the Blue Mountains in the east. In the west-central interior, the Cockpit Country is a maze of steep-sided karst hills and sinkholes that long sheltered the Maroons, escaped slaves who fought the British to a standstill and won treaties recognising their autonomy in 1739. Spain settled the island first, but England captured it in 1655 and turned it into one of its richest sugar colonies. Port Royal, the swaggering harbour town associated with buccaneers, largely slid into the sea during an earthquake in 1692. Slavery was abolished in the 1830s, and Jamaica became independent on 6 August 1962. Bauxite mining, tourism and remittances are the economic mainstays, and the island lies squarely in the path of Atlantic hurricanes, with Gilbert in 1988 among the most destructive in living memory.

facts: Mexico City is built on the drained bed of Lake Texcoco and is sinking by several centimetres a year.
Mexico is the world's largest producer of silver, and has been a major source of it since the Spanish colonial period.
Alongside Spanish it recognises 68 indigenous languages, spoken by several million people between them.
MX.about: Two great mountain chains, the Sierra Madre Occidental and Oriental, frame Mexico's high central plateau, which is capped in the south by the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt with peaks such as Popocatépetl. The north is dominated by the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts, the long Baja California peninsula encloses the Gulf of California, and in the south-east the flat limestone Yucatán has no surface rivers but thousands of water-filled sinkholes called cenotes; buried beneath its northern edge is the Chicxulub crater, linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs. Olmec, Maya, Zapotec and Aztec civilisations flourished here before Spanish forces captured Tenochtitlan in 1521. The independence struggle began in 1810 and succeeded in 1821. Mexico lost about half its territory to the United States after the war of 1846–48, and the revolution of 1910–20 reshaped its politics. Today it is a major manufacturing economy closely tied to US markets.

facts: Nicaragua is the largest country in Central America by area.
Lake Nicaragua is the biggest lake in Central America and holds freshwater sharks and sawfish.
Ometepe island in the lake is formed by two volcanoes joined by an isthmus.
NI.about: Western Nicaragua is a lowland strip punctuated by a line of volcanoes, among them Momotombo and Masaya, and dominated by two great lakes, Managua and Nicaragua, linked by the Tipitapa River. Behind them rise the central highlands, and to the east lies the broad, rainy Caribbean lowland of the Mosquito Coast, thinly populated and home to Miskito, Creole and other communities with a history of British influence. Independence from Spain came in 1821, and the country became a separate state in 1838. Rivalry between the colonial cities of León and Granada was so fierce that Managua was chosen as a compromise capital, and in the 1850s the American adventurer William Walker briefly seized power. Because the San Juan River and the lake offered a near-continuous water route between the oceans, a Nicaraguan canal was proposed for generations. The 20th century brought US occupation, the Somoza dynasty, the 1979 Sandinista revolution and the Contra war of the 1980s.

facts: The Panama Canal links the Atlantic and Pacific across 82 kilometres and carries a large share of world shipping.
Because of the isthmus's curve, the sun rises over the Pacific and sets over the Atlantic in Panama City.
The Darién Gap is the only break in the Pan-American Highway, an impassable stretch of rainforest and swamp.
PA.about: When the Isthmus of Panama rose from the sea about three million years ago, it joined North and South America, allowing animals to migrate between the continents and diverting ocean currents in ways that affected climate worldwide. The country is shaped like a flattened S, with a mountainous spine, the Bocas del Toro archipelago in the north-west, the Pearl Islands in the Gulf of Panama and the Guna Yala islands along the Caribbean coast, home to the self-governing Guna people. After independence from Spain in 1821, Panama joined Colombia, then broke away in 1903 with United States support; the US built the canal, opened in 1914, and controlled a surrounding zone until handing everything to Panama at the end of 1999. The economy is unusually service-based, built on canal revenue, logistics, banking, the Colón Free Zone and one of the world's largest ship registries.

facts: Saint Kitts and Nevis is the smallest sovereign state in the Americas by both area and population.
The two islands are separated by a strait about three kilometres wide.
Brimstone Hill Fortress is one of the best-preserved historic fortifications in the Americas.
KN.about: Both islands of this federation are volcanic. Saint Kitts has a mountainous spine with forested slopes and a low, dry south-eastern peninsula ending in salt ponds, while Nevis is almost entirely one cone-shaped peak whose summit is usually wrapped in cloud. In 1623 Thomas Warner established the first English colony in the Caribbean here, and French settlers arrived soon after; the two powers shared the island uneasily and in 1626 jointly massacred many of the Kalinago at Bloody Point. Sugar remained the backbone of the economy for more than three centuries, until the state-run industry closed in 2005. Nevis is the birthplace of Alexander Hamilton. Independence came on 19 September 1983 under a constitution that gives Nevis the right to secede; a 1998 referendum on separation fell just short of the required majority. The country launched one of the world's earliest citizenship-by-investment programmes in 1984, and tourism is now a major employer.

facts: The Pitons, two volcanic spires rising straight from the sea, are the island's defining landmark.
Saint Lucia changed hands between Britain and France fourteen times.
It has produced two Nobel laureates, giving it one of the highest rates per capita in the world.
LC.about: Saint Lucia is a mountainous volcanic island in the Windward chain, lying between Martinique and Saint Vincent, with rainforest covering its rugged interior. Near the town of Soufrière, the Sulphur Springs are part of a collapsed volcanic caldera, where visitors can approach steaming vents and bubbling mud pools. Kalinago resistance frustrated early English settlement attempts in the 17th century, and the island's sheltered harbours later made it a strategic prize; it passed finally to Britain in 1814. French influence nonetheless remains strong: most place names are French and Kwéyòl, a French-based creole, is widely spoken alongside English. Saint Lucia became independent on 22 February 1979. For much of the 20th century bananas were the main export, but the loss of preferential access to European markets pushed the economy towards tourism, which is now dominant, centred on the north-western coast around Rodney Bay and the historic military outpost at Pigeon Island.

facts: The country comprises the main island of Saint Vincent plus a chain of smaller Grenadines.
La Soufrière is an active volcano that erupted significantly in 1902 and again in 2021.
The Tobago Cays are a group of uninhabited islands inside a horseshoe reef.
VC.about: Saint Vincent is rugged, volcanic and densely forested, with black-sand beaches and fertile valleys on its slopes, while the Grenadines to the south are low, dry islands and cays such as Bequia, Mustique, Canouan and Union Island. Steep terrain and strong Indigenous resistance kept European colonists out longer than on most Caribbean islands, and the island was home to the Black Caribs, or Garifuna, descended from Kalinago and Africans. After the Carib Wars, the British deported most of them in 1797 to Roatán off Honduras, from where Garifuna communities spread along the Central American coast. Britain had gained the island in 1763, and independence came on 27 October 1979. Agriculture long dominated, with bananas and arrowroot, of which the island was once the world's leading producer. Tourism in the Grenadines, including the private island of Mustique, now matters greatly, and the Argyle International Airport, opened in 2017, improved direct access.

facts: Trinidad sits on the South American continental shelf and was joined to the mainland during the last ice age.
The Pitch Lake is the largest natural deposit of asphalt in the world.
The steelpan, developed in Trinidad in the 20th century, is one of the few acoustic instruments invented in modern times.
TT.about: The southernmost Caribbean state lies just off the Orinoco delta, and Trinidad's Northern Range is a geological continuation of Venezuela's coastal mountains. Smaller Tobago, about 30 kilometres to the north-east, has a forested central ridge and coral reefs. Spain held Trinidad until Britain captured it in 1797, while Tobago changed hands between European powers many times before the two colonies were joined in 1889. After slavery ended, Britain brought indentured labourers from India between 1845 and 1917, and today people of Indian and African descent form the two largest groups in roughly equal proportions, a mix that shapes the food, festivals and politics. Independence came on 31 August 1962, and the country became a republic in 1976. Unlike most of its neighbours, it is an industrial economy built on oil and natural gas, with liquefied natural gas, ammonia and methanol exports, and its Carnival, calypso and soca music are known worldwide.

facts: The United States spans six time zones across its states and territories, from Guam to Puerto Rico.
It has no official language at federal level, though English is used for government business.
Alaska alone would be the seventh largest country in the world if it were independent.
US.about: Between the old, worn Appalachians in the east and the high Rocky Mountains in the west lies the vast interior drained by the Mississippi–Missouri river system, one of the largest in the world, giving way westward to the Great Plains. Beyond the Rockies are the arid Great Basin, the Sierra Nevada and Cascades, and the Pacific coast, while Alaska and the volcanic islands of Hawaii lie far outside the main block of states. Thirteen British colonies declared independence on 4 July 1776, recognised by Britain in 1783, and the constitution adopted in 1787 remains in force. Expansion followed through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, war with Mexico in the 1840s and the purchase of Alaska in 1867, while the Civil War of 1861–65 ended slavery. The climate ranges from Arctic to tropical, with tornadoes on the plains and hurricanes along the Gulf coast. Immigration has shaped its population, and it has the world's largest economy.
